the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the fifth ply of the game. That is the longest defence Player 2 can force; the so-called 7-ply delay with 1... R2 5-4 is a miscounted blunder that in fact collapses back to the same 5-ply finish once the king walk is allowed. The forced win is therefore the classic five-ply, three-move rook mate.

3.text:
The file is a 1 dimensional position in which the only check giving piece
is the rook.  With

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

K1 is safe because R1 blocks the R2–K1 line and K2 is safe because N2
blocks the R1–K2 line.  The only first move which does not at once lose
material and which does not leave K1 in the R2 line is

1. N1 1–3

K1 0–R1 2 still blocks R2 5 and the knight now screens the 3 square.
R1×5 is a draw by stalemate and any R1 advance on the first move loses
tempo.  After 1.N1–3 Black has three legal continuations.

*1… R2 5×3* is the immediate sacrifice.  2.R1 2×3 is a stalemate
because N2 6 still blocks the R1–K2 line and Black has no legal move,
so White is forced to 2.R1 2–1.  After 2.R1–1 Black can interpose with
R2 and the mate is forced on the third White move, 5 plies in all.

*1… R2 5–4* is the first stalling try.  With the rook on 4 the
R1–K2 line is still blocked by N1 3.  The only useful reply is
2.R1 2–1, 2…R2 4×3, 3.R1 1×3, 3…N2 6–4, 4.R1 3×4#
and the rook is on 4 with the clear line 4–5–6–7.  K2 7–6 would stay
on the R1–K2 line and is illegal by the King-safety rule, there is no
interposition and no capture.  This is a 7-ply, 4 White-move defence.

The maximal defence is

1… N2 6–4

The knight is now on the only square which can keep K2 out of the
R1-line after the first interposition.  White must now clear the
centre.  The essentially forced continuation with best defence is

2. N1 3×5   2… K2 7–6
3. R1 2–4   3… N2 4–6
4. N1 5–3   4… N2 6–4
5. R1 4×6

R1 is now on 6 with K2 on 7, the line 6–7 is clear, K2 7–6 is onto the
checking rook and therefore illegal under King Safety, K2 cannot take,
and Black has no interposing man.  In plies

1 N1–3   1… N2–4
2 N1×5   2… K2–6
3 R1–4   3… N2–6
4 N1–3   4… N2–4
5 R1×6   #

the mate is delivered on the ninth half-move of the game, i.e. on the
fifth move of the first player.  In ordinary “one half-move = one turn’’
counting this is turn 9 of the game, the well known mate in 5 for
White.  Counting only the moves of the winning side the forced win is
five White moves, the three-move 5-ply line

1.N1–3 1…R2×3 2.R1–1 2…N2–4 3.R1×4#

being the absolute fastest mate. ∎

10.text:
On the 1-D file the only checking piece is a rook and the only
interpositors that can be kept between R1 and K2 are R2 and N2.
After

1 N1 1-3

K1 is screened by R1 and the  R2-K1  line is blocked by the knight on 3.
Up to symmetry the only defence which does not give the
text book

1... R2 5x3 2 R1 2x3 2... N2 6-4 3 R1 3x4#

mate in five plies is a pure stalling defence.  With

1... R2 5-4    1... N2 6-4

Black can keep a man on the 3-5 corridor and can shuttle the
knight 6-4-6-4... so that the line

R1 - . - R2 - N2 - K2

never becomes completely clear.  The first useful White improvement
is the centralisation of the rook.  The longest defence that can be
kept is e.g.

1 N1 1-3 1... N2 6-4
2 R1 2-4 2... N2 4-6
3 N1 3-5 3... N2 6-4
4 R1 4-5 4... K2 7-6
5 R1 5-6 5... R2 5-4
6 N1 5-3 6... R2 4-5
7 R1 6xN2 7... R2 5-4
8 N1 3-5 8... R2 4-3
9 R1 6-7xK2#

in ply notation.  The ninth ply of the game is the fifth move of
Player 1.  In the ordinary alternating 1,2,3,... half-move counting
that is the 9th turn of the game, the mate being delivered on P1's
5th move.  In White-move counting this is the familiar
``mate in five'' , the five-move, nine-ply, forced win.  The
text-book sacrifice 1... R2 5x3 2 R1 2x3 2... N2 6-4 3 R1 3x4# is the
five-ply, three-White-move shortest line.

2.text:
On the 1–file a check can only be given by the rook and a King may never
be left on the same open file as the enemy rook.  Up to symmetry the
only first move which does not throw the R1 away at once is

*1. N1 1–3*

K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the Knight now stands on the
3–square.  The three moves which do not lose at once for Black are

*1… R2 5×3* , *1… R2 5–4* and *1… N2 6–4*.

*1…R2×N1* is the immediate zugzwang

1. N1–3 1…R2×N1 2. R1×R2 2…N2 6–4 3. R1×N2#

R1 4–7 is now open, K2 7–6 would stay on the R1–line and is illegal by
the King-safety rule and Black has no interposition.  The mate is
delivered on White’s third move, the fifth ply of the game, the usual
text-book “mate in three”

1 N1 1–3  R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3   N2 6–4
3 R1 3×4  #

If Black refuses the bait the knight can be shuttled 6↔4 and the rook
can be interposed on 4–5 for a few tempi.  With best stalling the
defence is

1. N1 1–3  1…N2 6–4
2. R1 2–1  2…R2 5–4
3. N1 3–1  3…R2 4–3
4. R1 1×3  4…N2 6–4
5. R1 3–4  5…

and the line can be continued with the forced N2 4↔6 shuffle and the
R2 3↔4 interpositions until the screen is finally taken away on
White’s fifth move.  In full-ply counting the last mating move is made
on the ninth ply of the game, i.e. on White’s fifth move, the
9-ply/5-move maximal forced win.  The 5-ply, three-White-move line
above is the shortest forced mate, normally quoted as the five-ply
mate in three. ∎

11.text:
The only first move which does not give the R1 away at once is the
interposition

1. N1 1-3

K1 0 - R2 5 is still covered by R1 2 and the knight now sits in front
of the rook so that R1 is shut in on the right by its own man.  
After 1.N1-3 the only defence which does not lose at once is the
sacrifice on the interposition square

1... R2 5x3

K2 7 is still covered by N2 6 and R1 2 - K2 7 is still blocked by the
new R2 3.  Now

2. R1 2x3

is forced.  K1 is safe because the enemy rook has disappeared and R1
is now on the same rank as K2.  The only man which can still keep K2
out of the R1 line is the knight and

2... N2 6-4

is the only king-safe move, K2 7-6 would still lie on the R1 3 - K2 7
line and is illegal by the King-safety rule.  After 2... N2-4 the line
R1 3 - K2 7 is

3 - 4 N2 - 5 - 6 - 7

and the knight is the unique cover.  White now removes the cover

3. R1 3x4

R1 is now on 4 and the line 4-5-6-7 is clear.  K2 is in rook check.
K2 7-6 would still be on the R1 4 - 7 line and is therefore illegal
by King-safety, K2 cannot take on 4 and Black has no other man with
which to interpose or to capture the checking rook.  Black has no
legal move with his king in check.

In ply notation

1 N1 1-3    1... R2 5-3xN1
2 R1 2-3xR2 2... N2 6-4
3 R1 3-4xN2 #

the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the fifth half-move of
the game.  In the usual “one move = one turn’’ convention this is the
5th turn of the game, i.e. the third turn - the third move - of Player
1.  With the customary “one round = one turn’’ convention it is the
text-book three-turn, three-move rook mate. ∎

8.text:
On the file the only checking piece is a rook and a move is legal only if the
moving side's own King stays off the Rook line of the opponent.

*1.N1 1-3* is the only White first move which does not at once lose the
R1 or give Black a stalemate.  After

```
0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

K1 is still screened by R1 on 2 and K2 is still screened by N1 on 3, so the
move is legal.

With best defence Black can keep the central screen alive.  The longest
defence which can be kept legal under the King–Safety rule is

1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-1          K1 is now screened by R1 on 1
2...R2 4xN1 3
3.R1 1xR2 3
3...N2 6-4        N2 is the only piece which can still interpose on
                  3-7 and 4 still screens K2 from R1 3
4.R1 3xN2 4#

After 4.R1xN2

```
0 K1 . . . R1 . . 7 K2
```

R1 4 attacks K2 7 on the clear line 4-5-6-7.  K2 7-6 would stay on the
R1-line 4-5-6 and is illegal by King-Safety, K2 cannot take on 4 and there
is no interposing man left.  Black has no legal move with his King in
rook check.

In ply notation the forced line is

1.N1 1-3  1...R2 5-4   2.R1 2-1  2...R2 4xN1 3   3.R1 1xR2 3
3...N2 6-4            4.R1 3xN2 4#

i.e. White mates on his 4th – and with the usual king shuffle
7-6/5-6 rook interposition on 5 – on his 5th move of the game.  In
half-move counting this is the 7–9 ply mate

1 N1-3  R2 5-3xN1  2 R1 2xR2 3  2...N2 6-4  3 R1 3xN2 4#

the familiar 5-ply, three White-move, mate.  The normal
text-book minimal forced mate is therefore

1.N1 1-3  R2 5x3  2.R1 2xR2  2...N2 6-4  3.R1 3xN2#

delivered on White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply of the game.  With optimal
stalling the mate can be forced on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the
game, the 9-turn line quoted in the literature. ∎

6.text:
The only first move which does not lose material at once or give P2 an
immediate draw is

*1. N1 1-3*

K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the king is safe.  After
1.N1-3 P2 has the three essentially different replies

* 1…R2 5×3 , 1…R2 5-4 , 1…N2 6-4 .

1…R2×N1 is the fastest line

1. N1 1-3   1…R2 5×3
2. R1 2×3
2…N2 6-4
3. R1 3×4 #

and after 3.R1×N2 the R1 is now on 4 with the line 4-5-6-7 clear.
K2 7 is in rook check, K2 7-6 would stay on the 4-7 line and is illegal
by the King-safety rule, there is no interposition and no capture.
In ply notation this is

1 P1 N1 1-3
2 P2 R2 5-3×N1
3 P1 R1 2-3×R2
4 P2 N2 6-4
5 P1 R1 3-4×N2 #

i.e. three White moves, five plies in all.  In the usual “mate in three’’
counting this is the three-move mate.

Against best stalling P2 can keep the centre closed with the
1…R2 5-4 / N2 6-4 shuffles.  Up to the usual transpositions the
longest defence which does not allow the five-ply line above is

1 N1 1-3      1…R2 5-4
2 R1 2-1      2…R2 4-5
3 N1 3-5      3…R2 5-4
4 R1 1-2      4…N2 6-4
5 R1 2-4×N2 #

which is the same mating idea reached on White’s fifth move.  In
half-move counting this is the ninth ply of the game, the fifth move of
Player 1, the normal “mate in five’’ with optimal defence.  The
five-ply / three-move line above is the shortest forced mate; with the
convention that a turn is a half-move the maximally stalled forced win
is delivered on the 9th ply, i.e. on Player 1’s 5th move, the classic
five-ply mate in three White moves. ∎

4.text:
On the file a check can be given only by a rook and a king can be kept
safe only by interposing on the rook line.  After

* 1. N1 1-3

the K1–R2 line is still covered by R1 2 and the K2–R1 line is now
covered by N1 3.  The three legal replies of Black are

* 1… R2 5×3 N1
* 1… R2 5-4
* 1… N2 6-4 .

The first is the quickest loss.  The two delaying replies are
essentially the same and with best play the position can be forced
to the familiar

```
0 K1  1 .  2 R1  3 N1  4 N2  5 R2  6 .  7 K2
```

After 1… N2 6-4 the cheapest White reply is 2. R1 2-1.  Black can now
only shuffle the rook and the knight on the 4-6 corridor.  One
maximally stalling line is

1. N1 1-3         1… N2 6-4
2. R1 2-1         2… R2 5-6
3. N1 3-5         3… N2 4-2
4. R1 1×2 N2      4… R2 6×5 N1
5. R1 2×5 R2 #

i.e. in plies

1 P1 N1 1-3
2 P2 N2 6-4
3 P1 R1 2-1
4 P2 R2 5-6
5 P1 N1 3-5
6 P2 N2 4-2
7 P1 R1 1×2
8 P2 R2 6×5
9 P1 R1 2×5

After 9. R1 5 K2 is in rook check on the clear line 5-6-7.  
K2 7-6 would stay on the R1 line and is illegal by the King–Safety
rule, K2 cannot capture on 5 and there is no interposing man left.
Black has no legal move with his king in check.  This is the ordinary
rook mate on 4.

In the usual half-move counting the mate is delivered on the 9th ply
of the game, the 5th move of the first player.  Counting a half-move
as a turn this is the 9-turn forced win, three turns for the first
player in the very quick 1… R2×N1 defence and five White moves,
nine plies in total, in the maximally stalling defence.  The
text-book 5-ply, three-move mate

1. N1 1-3  1… R2 5×3
2. R1 2×3  2… N2 6-4
3. R1 3×4 #

is the minimal forced mate, five plies, three White moves. ∎

12.text:
On the 8-point file a check can only be given by a rook and a check
to K2 can only be given by R1 on the left of 7 with the squares between
it and 7 empty.  In the initial

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

K1 is safe because N1 1 and R1 2 interpose on the R2–K1 line and K2 is
safe because N2 6 and R2 5 interpose on the R1–K2 line.

The first useful first move is the opening

1. N1 1–3

K1 is still covered by R1 and the R2–K1 line is now blocked on 3.
Up to symmetry the only delaying defence is

1… R2 5–4

and now

2. N1 3–5

is forced.  With best play Black is forced to give up the centre

2… R2 4×5

and now

3. R1 2×5

removes the second rook.  The position is

K1 0       R1 5       N2 6       K2 7

K2 is still covered by N2.  Black is forced

3… N2 6–4

because K2 7–6 would be on the R1 line and after the move the line
R1–K2 is

R1 5 – 6 – 7

with the interposing square 6 empty.  The mate is

4. R1 5×4 #

R1 is now on 4 and the line 4–5–6–7 is clear.  K2 is in rook check,
K2 7–6 would still be on the rook line 4–6 and is therefore illegal by
the King–safety rule, there is no interposition left and there is no
capture of the checking rook.  In half-move notation the longest
forced line that can be obtained against best stalling defence is

1. N1 1–3   1… R2 5–4
2. N1 3–5   2… R2 4×5
3. R1 2×5   3… N2 6–4
4. R1 5×4 #

i.e. the mate is delivered on the 7th half-move of the game, the
fourth move of the first player.  The textbook shortest forced line is
the familiar

1. N1 1–3   1… R2 5×3
2. R1 2×3   2… N2 6–4
3. R1 3×4 #

which is the 5-ply, three-move mate, the third move of Player 1, the
fifth ply of the game.  This is the mate that is normally quoted as
the three-move rook mate. ∎

public_text.1:
The N1 1-3 opening is forced and the king-safety pin is the whole game.

After 1. N1 1-3 K1 is still covered by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now blocked by the knight on 3. The immediate 1... R2 5x3 is a blunder. It hands White the rook exchange 2. R1 2x3 and leaves Black with only N2 to screen K2. That is the 5-ply textbook line, which is why it keeps coming up, but it is not best defence.

The best stalling defence is to keep the screen on the king and to keep a piece between R1 and K2 for as long as possible:

1. N1 1-3
1... N2 6-4

N2 6-4 is the only move that does not present the rook with an immediate clear line. 1... R2 5-4 is too slow and 1... R2 x N1 loses the rook at once. With N2 on 4 the line  R1 2 - K2 7 is still blocked.

2. R1 2-5 x R2

R1 can now take the rook on 5 through 3,4. K1 is safe: R2 is gone, so the King-safety rule is satisfied. The rook is on 5 with a direct shot to K2 on 7 except for the knight on 4.

2... N2 4-6

The only way to restore a screen is to put the knight back on 6.  N2 4-2 would walk into N1 x 7 and 2... K2 7-6 is illegal by king safety because K2 would remain on the R1 5 line.

3. N1 3-5

The knight now ties N2 down and threatens N1 5-7. White cannot yet mate because N2 on 6 still blocks the 5-7 line.

3... N2 6-4

Any other retreat loses the king at once. 4-4 is forced.

4. R1 5-6 x N2

The rook now sits on 6 with a direct line to K2 on 7. The move is king-safe: R2 is gone and the only remaining black piece is K2.

4... is now essentially a stall. K2 cannot move to 6 because 6 is occupied by the checking rook and K2 7-5 would stay on the rook line 6-5 and is illegal by king safety. The only legal second player move is the meaningless king shuffle that keeps the king out of a discovered attack, which with optimal play is K2 7-6 only to immediately walk back.

5. R1 6-7 x K2

With the knight gone the line 4-5-6-7 is clear and the rook mates on 7. K2 has no flight square, no interposition and no capture.

Counting half moves this is

1 N1-3 1... N2-4
2 R1xR5 2... N2-6
3 N1-5 3... N2-4
4 R1xN6 4... stall
5 R1xK7

i.e. the ninth ply of the game, the fifth move of Player 1. The extra two plies compared with the R2 x N1 blunder are exactly the N2 6-4 / 6-4 shuttle that optimal defence can force. That is the longest forced win, 9 plies in total under perfect stalling.
public_text.13:
The mate is forced on the 5th ply, i.e. White’s third move. The only first move that does not lose R1 at once is

1. N1 1-3

K1 is still covered by R1 on 2 and the R2-K1 line is still blocked by R1. Any R1 advance 2→4 loses tempo and lets R2 come out, and R1×5 is premature because N2 can re-block.

The only defence that keeps Black alive is

1… R2 5-3 x N1

1… R2 5-4 is not a real delay. After 1…R2 5-4 White has 2. K1 0-1 and the rook line to K2 is already open to a future R1×R2, so the position is worse for Black and the mate is reached even faster. With best defence Black must take.

After 1…R2×N1 White recaptures at once

2. R1 2-3 x R2

K1 is safe, the enemy rook is gone and R1 is now on the same rank as K2. K2 7-6 is illegal before the knight moves because N2 on 6 covers 6, and any rook move is impossible. The only move that keeps K2 out of the R1 line is

2… N2 6-4

N2 6-2 is impossible because R1 on 3 covers 4-7, and K2 cannot move.

Now the only screen left is the knight on 4. 

3. R1 3-4 x N2 # 

R1 now attacks K2 on 7 on the clear line 4-5-6-7. K2 7-6 would stay on the R1 line 4-7 and is illegal under King Safety, K2 cannot capture on 4, and there is no interposing piece. The position is a pure rook checkmate.

In ply notation:
1 N1 1-3 1…R2×N1
2 R1×R2 2…N2 6-4
3 R1×N2 #

That is three moves for Player 1, five half-moves in total. The 9-ply lines that are being quoted require K2 to move onto a square still covered by R1, e.g. K2 7-6 after the rook is on 4 or 6, which is illegal by the King Safety rule, and they also allow non-forced interpositions with R2 that would leave K1 in attack from R2 through N1. Once the king-safety rule is applied strictly the knight shuffles collapse and the same R1×N2 mate is forced. The so-called 7-ply longest defence is a miscount of the same 5-ply line; the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the fifth turn of the game.
public_text.5:
The 5-ply textbook line is not the forced line under perfect defence, it is the fastest line after Black cooperates by taking on 3 at once.

The real point is that 1.N1 1-3 does not force 1…R2 5x3. Black can keep the screen intact with 1…R2 5-4. After 1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5-4 the White king is still safe because R1 2 still blocks R2-K1 and the knight now screens the 3-square. White cannot take on 5 yet, the only useful follow up is 2.K1 0-1 to keep the king off the future rook line and to free the 0-square for later development.

Now 2…R2 4-3xN1 is forced to maintain pressure, and 3.R1 2x3 recovers the rook. The position is

K1 1 . R1 3 . . N2 6 K2 7

and the only Black man that can still interpose is N2. 3…N2 6-4 is the only king-safe move, K2 7-6 would still leave K2 on the R1 line 3-7.

From here White has to finish the clearance. 4.R1 3-4 opens 4-7 but the knight is now on 4, so 4…N2 4-6 restores the screen. 5.N1 3-5 improves the net and ties N2 down. Black is forced to 5…N2 6-4 again, any other retreat walks into N1x7.

Now 6.R1 4x6xN2 is the decisive clearance. R1 on 6 gives immediate rook check on K2 7, K2 7-6 is illegal by King Safety because 6 is covered by the checking rook, and K2 7-5 is illegal because 5 is on the rook line 6-7. R2 can interpose on 4, so Black gets one last tempo with 6…R2 3-4.

7.N1 5-? actually 7.N1 3-5 was already played; after the interposition the correct improvement is 7.N1 5-? The continuation that keeps K1 safe is 7.N1 5-? I will compress: after the interposition White forces the king shuffle 7…K2 7-6 is illegal, so Black can only shuffle R2 back to unblock K1, 7…R2 4-5. 

8.R1 6-7 is now mate in the sense that the rook covers 7 and the knight on 5 covers 6 and the rook on 5 is pinned to its own king by the White knight. The only legal Black move left is the meaningless R2 5-2 which re-exposes K1 to the rook line and is illegal by King Safety.

The final mating capture R1xK2 is then delivered on the 9th ply, i.e. on White’s 5th move. That is the longest defence Black can force: the knight can shuttle 6-4-6-4, the rook can retreat 5-4-3, and the king shuffle 7-6-5 is forbidden by King Safety, so the extra three plies are unavoidable.

In other words the 5-ply mate 1.N1 1-3 1…R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2…N2 6-4 3.R1xN2 # relies on Black taking the bait on move 1. With the optimal delaying defence 1…R2 5-4 the mate is pushed to the seventh ply of the textbook score and to the ninth ply in total alternating counting, which is the forced win the second player can be made to concede to. Counting every half-move as a turn, that is a forced win in 9 turns.
public_text.14:
The forced mate is the classic N1 1-3 opening and it cannot be delayed beyond the fifth ply.

1. N1 1-3
K1 is still covered by R1 2 and the rook line 0-5 is now blocked by the knight on 3. Any other first move loses material to R2 5-2 or opens K1 to R2.

The only defence that does not lose on the spot is
1… R2 5×3
If R2 stays on 5 White gets R1 2-5 next move with a direct rook line to K2 and N2 cannot block on 6 in time. If N2 moves first, N2 6-4 leaves the 5-square open and R1 2-5 mates immediately. So 1…R2×N1 is forced.

2. R1 2×3
K1 is now safe because the enemy rook is gone. R1 is on 3 with a clear line to K2 7 blocked only by N2 6.

2… N2 6-4
is forced. K2 7-6 is illegal by king safety: R1 3 would still attack the 6-square, and K2 would remain on the same rook line 3-7. Any rook move is impossible and N2 cannot go to 2. N2 6-4 is the only square that keeps K2 out of the rook line.

Now the position is
K1 0 . R1 3 . . N2 4 . K2 7
with squares 5 and 6 empty between R1 and K2.

3. R1 3×4
R1 now sits on 4 and gives a rook check on the line 4-5-6-7. K2 cannot capture, cannot interpose and cannot move:
* K2 7-6 is illegal: 6 is on the rook line 4-7 and would leave the king under attack from R1 4.
* K2 7-8 is off board.
* The only remaining piece, N2, is gone.

That is checkmate on White’s third move, the fifth ply of the game.

The 9-ply stalling lines that are being quoted require illegal king moves. Once R1 is on 5 or 4 the moves K2 7-6, K2 6-5, K2 5-6 etc. all leave K2 on the rook line of R1 and are prohibited by the King Safety rule. The king shuffles that give the “9-turn” count are therefore not legal, and the N2 6-4 retreat is fatal, not delaying.

In normal ply counting the mate is therefore forced on ply 5, i.e. the third move of Player 1. Counting a full round as one turn that is the third turn of Player 1, five half-moves in total.
public_text.7:
The mate is forced by the N1 sacrifice and it is forced much sooner than the later K1 shuffling lines suggest.

1. N1 1-3
The knight blocks the R2–K1 line and prepares the R1 corridor.  K1 0 is still covered by R1 2 and the move is the only first move that does not lose R1 at once.

2…R2 5×3 is the only defence that does not lose on the spot.  Any R2 retreat such as 1…R2 5-4 leaves the rook on a square that White can exploit with the same sacrifice and it in fact shortens the defence, it does not lengthen it.  After the capture the position is

K1 0 . R1×R2 3 . . . N2 6 K2 7

with the enemy rook gone.

2. R1 2×3
K1 is now safe because there is no longer an enemy rook, and R1 is on the same rank as K2.  The only remaining defender of K2 is N2 on 6.

2…N2 6-4
K2 7-6 is illegal: 6 would still be on the R1 3–K2 7 line and the king-safety rule forbids moving the king into a rook line.  Every other N2 move walks into R1×N2 at once, so 6-4 is forced.

3. R1 3×4
R1 is now on 4 with a clear rook line 4-5-6-7 to K2.  K2 is in rook check.  K2 7-6 is illegal by king-safety because 6 is covered by R1, K2 cannot capture on 4, and there is no interposing piece left.  Black has no legal move and the king is in check.

In ply notation

1 N1 1-3   1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3   2…N2 6-4
3 R1 3×4#

That is White’s third move, the fifth ply of the game.  Counting only the moves of the player who is trying to win it is a three-move mate, five half-moves in total.  The 7-ply lines that require White to insert a waiting K1 0-1 after 1…R2 5-4 are not a genuine stall: the retreat 1…R2 5-4 does not prevent the same sacrifice and the extra waiting move is not forced against best defence.  With correct king-safety enforcement the sacrifice line above is forced and the mate is delivered on the 5th ply.

The opening is forced. After K1 N1 R1 . . R2 N2 K2 the only first move that keeps K1 safe and opens a line on the right is

1. N1 1-3

R1 is still on 2 so R2 5-0 is blocked and K1 is safe. Anything else with R1 loses the rook at once or walks K1 into the R2 line.

With N1 on 3 the only defence that does not lose the rook on the next move is the immediate exchange

1... R2 5-3 x N1

1... R2 5-4 is not a defence at all. It moves the screening rook one square closer to K1 and leaves the same interposition on 3, so White can simply walk the king to 1 and then win back on 3 with tempo. In practice it is a losing tempo that allows White to finish the same way one ply faster than the main line, so it cannot be the maximal stall.

Now

2. R1 2-3 x R2

is forced and legal; K1 is safe because the opponent rook is gone. The only man that can still keep K2 out of the R1 line is the knight.

2... N2 6-4

is forced. K2 7-6 would stay on the 3-7 line and is illegal by king safety, and any rook move is impossible. After 2... N2 6-4 the line R1 3 - K2 7 is 3 - 4(N2) - 5 - 6 - 7.

3. R1 3-4 x N2

Mate. R1 is now on 4 with the clear line 4-5-6-7 to K2. K2 cannot take, K2 7-6 would still be on the rook line 4-6 and is illegal by the king-safety rule, there is no interposition left and no second piece to capture the checking rook.

In plies

1 N1 1-3
1... R2 5-3 x N1
2 R1 2-3 x R2
2... N2 6-4
3 R1 3-4 x N2 #

the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the fifth ply of the game. That is the longest defence Player 2 can force; the so-called 7-ply delay with 1... R2 5-4 is a miscounted blunder that in fact collapses back to the same 5-ply finish once the king walk is allowed. The forced win is therefore the classic five-ply, three-move rook mate.

The file is a 1 dimensional position in which the only check giving piece
is the rook.  With

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

K1 is safe because R1 blocks the R2–K1 line and K2 is safe because N2
blocks the R1–K2 line.  The only first move which does not at once lose
material and which does not leave K1 in the R2 line is

1. N1 1–3

K1 0–R1 2 still blocks R2 5 and the knight now screens the 3 square.
R1×5 is a draw by stalemate and any R1 advance on the first move loses
tempo.  After 1.N1–3 Black has three legal continuations.

*1… R2 5×3* is the immediate sacrifice.  2.R1 2×3 is a stalemate
because N2 6 still blocks the R1–K2 line and Black has no legal move,
so White is forced to 2.R1 2–1.  After 2.R1–1 Black can interpose with
R2 and the mate is forced on the third White move, 5 plies in all.

*1… R2 5–4* is the first stalling try.  With the rook on 4 the
R1–K2 line is still blocked by N1 3.  The only useful reply is
2.R1 2–1, 2…R2 4×3, 3.R1 1×3, 3…N2 6–4, 4.R1 3×4#
and the rook is on 4 with the clear line 4–5–6–7.  K2 7–6 would stay
on the R1–K2 line and is illegal by the King-safety rule, there is no
interposition and no capture.  This is a 7-ply, 4 White-move defence.

The maximal defence is

1… N2 6–4

The knight is now on the only square which can keep K2 out of the
R1-line after the first interposition.  White must now clear the
centre.  The essentially forced continuation with best defence is

2. N1 3×5   2… K2 7–6
3. R1 2–4   3… N2 4–6
4. N1 5–3   4… N2 6–4
5. R1 4×6

R1 is now on 6 with K2 on 7, the line 6–7 is clear, K2 7–6 is onto the
checking rook and therefore illegal under King Safety, K2 cannot take,
and Black has no interposing man.  In plies

1 N1–3   1… N2–4
2 N1×5   2… K2–6
3 R1–4   3… N2–6
4 N1–3   4… N2–4
5 R1×6   #

the mate is delivered on the ninth half-move of the game, i.e. on the

counting this is turn 9 of the game, the well known mate in 5 for
White.  Counting only the moves of the winning side the forced win is

1.N1–3 1…R2×3 2.R1–1 2…N2–4 3.R1×4#

being the absolute fastest mate. ∎

On the 1–file a check can only be given by the rook and a King may never
be left on the same open file as the enemy rook.  Up to symmetry the
only first move which does not throw the R1 away at once is

*1. N1 1–3*

K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the Knight now stands on the
3–square.  The three moves which do not lose at once for Black are

*1… R2 5×3* , *1… R2 5–4* and *1… N2 6–4*.

*1…R2×N1* is the immediate zugzwang

1. N1–3 1…R2×N1 2. R1×R2 2…N2 6–4 3. R1×N2#

R1 4–7 is now open, K2 7–6 would stay on the R1–line and is illegal by
the King-safety rule and Black has no interposition.  The mate is
delivered on White’s third move, the fifth ply of the game, the usual
text-book “mate in three”

1 N1 1–3  R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3   N2 6–4
3 R1 3×4  #

If Black refuses the bait the knight can be shuttled 6↔4 and the rook
can be interposed on 4–5 for a few tempi.  With best stalling the
defence is

1. N1 1–3  1…N2 6–4
2. R1 2–1  2…R2 5–4
3. N1 3–1  3…R2 4–3
4. R1 1×3  4…N2 6–4
5. R1 3–4  5…

and the line can be continued with the forced N2 4↔6 shuffle and the
R2 3↔4 interpositions until the screen is finally taken away on
White’s fifth move.  In full-ply counting the last mating move is made
on the ninth ply of the game, i.e. on White’s fifth move, the
9-ply/5-move maximal forced win.  The 5-ply, three-White-move line
above is the shortest forced mate, normally quoted as the five-ply
mate in three. ∎

On the file the only checking piece is a rook and a move is legal only if the
moving side's own King stays off the Rook line of the opponent.

*1.N1 1-3* is the only White first move which does not at once lose the
R1 or give Black a stalemate.  After

```
0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

K1 is still screened by R1 on 2 and K2 is still screened by N1 on 3, so the
move is legal.

With best defence Black can keep the central screen alive.  The longest
defence which can be kept legal under the King–Safety rule is

1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-1          K1 is now screened by R1 on 1
2...R2 4xN1 3
3.R1 1xR2 3
3...N2 6-4        N2 is the only piece which can still interpose on
                  3-7 and 4 still screens K2 from R1 3
4.R1 3xN2 4#

After 4.R1xN2

```
0 K1 . . . R1 . . 7 K2
```

R1 4 attacks K2 7 on the clear line 4-5-6-7.  K2 7-6 would stay on the
R1-line 4-5-6 and is illegal by King-Safety, K2 cannot take on 4 and there
is no interposing man left.  Black has no legal move with his King in
rook check.

In ply notation the forced line is

1.N1 1-3  1...R2 5-4   2.R1 2-1  2...R2 4xN1 3   3.R1 1xR2 3
3...N2 6-4            4.R1 3xN2 4#

i.e. White mates on his 4th – and with the usual king shuffle
7-6/5-6 rook interposition on 5 – on his 5th move of the game.  In
half-move counting this is the 7–9 ply mate

1 N1-3  R2 5-3xN1  2 R1 2xR2 3  2...N2 6-4  3 R1 3xN2 4#

the familiar 5-ply, three White-move, mate.  The normal
text-book minimal forced mate is therefore

1.N1 1-3  R2 5x3  2.R1 2xR2  2...N2 6-4  3.R1 3xN2#

delivered on White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply of the game.  With optimal
stalling the mate can be forced on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the
game, the 9-turn line quoted in the literature. ∎

The only first move which does not lose material at once or give P2 an
immediate draw is

*1. N1 1-3*

K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the king is safe.  After
1.N1-3 P2 has the three essentially different replies

* 1…R2 5×3 , 1…R2 5-4 , 1…N2 6-4 .

1…R2×N1 is the fastest line

1. N1 1-3   1…R2 5×3
2. R1 2×3
2…N2 6-4

convention that a turn is a half-move the maximally stalled forced win

On the file a check can be given only by a rook and a king can be kept
safe only by interposing on the rook line.  After

* 1. N1 1-3

the K1–R2 line is still covered by R1 2 and the K2–R1 line is now
covered by N1 3.  The three legal replies of Black are

* 1… R2 5×3 N1
* 1… R2 5-4
* 1… N2 6-4 .

The first is the quickest loss.  The two delaying replies are
essentially the same and with best play the position can be forced
to the familiar

```
0 K1  1 .  2 R1  3 N1  4 N2  5 R2  6 .  7 K2
```

After 1… N2 6-4 the cheapest White reply is 2. R1 2-1.  Black can now
only shuffle the rook and the knight on the 4-6 corridor.  One
maximally stalling line is

1. N1 1-3         1… N2 6-4
2. R1 2-1         2… R2 5-6
3. N1 3-5         3… N2 4-2
4. R1 1×2 N2      4… R2 6×5 N1
5. R1 2×5 R2 #

i.e. in plies

1 P1 N1 1-3
2 P2 N2 6-4
3 P1 R1 2-1
4 P2 R2 5-6
5 P1 N1 3-5
6 P2 N2 4-2
7 P1 R1 1×2
8 P2 R2 6×5
9 P1 R1 2×5

After 9. R1 5 K2 is in rook check on the clear line 5-6-7.  
K2 7-6 would stay on the R1 line and is illegal by the King–Safety
rule, K2 cannot capture on 5 and there is no interposing man left.
Black has no legal move with his king in check.  This is the ordinary
rook mate on 4.

In the usual half-move counting the mate is delivered on the 9th ply
of the game, the 5th move of the first player.  Counting a half-move
as a turn this is the 9-turn forced win, three turns for the first
player in the very quick 1… R2×N1 defence and five White moves,
nine plies in total, in the maximally stalling defence.  The
text-book 5-ply, three-move mate

1. N1 1-3  1… R2 5×3
2. R1 2×3  2… N2 6-4
3. R1 3×4 #

is the minimal forced mate, five plies, three White moves. ∎

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position is essentially a rook-mate on a line. K1 0, N1 1, R1 2 vs R2 5, N2 6, K2 7, with 3,4 empty. King-safety forbids leaving own King on an open rook line of the opponent.

First move is forced up to equivalence:
* K1 has no safe move.
* R1→3/4 or R1×5 loses tempo / gives stalemate.
* N1 1-3 blocks the R2–R1 line and keeps K1 safe via R1 2. This is the unique winning first move.

After 1.N1-3 the board is 0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2.

P2 essentially has three different replies: R2×N1 on 3, R2 5-4, N2 6-4.

Fastest textbook line:
1 N1-3 1… R2×N1 2 R1×R2 2… N2 6-4 3 R1×N2 #.
After 2.R1×R2 the enemy rook is gone, K1 is safe. N2 6-4 is the only king-safe move; K2 7-6 stays on the R1 3–7 line and is illegal by King Safety. R1 on 4 now checks K2 on 7 on clear line 4-5-6-7, K2 7-6 stays on the line and is illegal, no interposition/capture. This is 5 plies, White’s 3rd move.

Stalling defence:
The R2×N1 line is the fastest loss. Best stalling is to keep a screen on K2 and to shuttle N2. With 1…N2 6-4 or 1…R2 5-4 the N2 6-4 ↔ 6 shuttle and R2 5-4 ↔ 3-4 interpositions can add tempi. The maximally stalled line quoted in the room is

1 N1-3 1…N2 6-4
2 R1 2-5×R2 2…N2 4-6
3 N1 3-5 3…N2 6-4
4 R1 5-6×N2 4… stall
5 R1 6-7×K2

i.e. 9 plies, White’s 5th move. Same idea appears as 1…R2 5-4 2 R1 2-1 2…R2 4×N1 etc., leading to a mate on White’s 4th/5th move, 7-9 ply total.

Disagreement in the room is twofold:
* Counting convention: 5 plies = 3 White moves = “mate in three”. Many colleagues call this “5 turns”. Others count a half-move as a turn and call the maximal stall “9 turns”, i.e. 9 plies / 5 White moves.
* Legality of the long stalling lines. Several colleagues argue that the king shuffles K2 7-6, 6-5 etc. that appear in some 9-ply scores are illegal by King Safety once R1 is on 4/5/6, and that after proper enforcement the N2 shuttle collapses to the 5-ply mate. Others defend the 9-ply line as legal because the extra tempi are obtained by piece shuffles, not by illegal king moves, with the final mate delivered on R1 6-7×K2 after the N2 screen is removed.

Current best synthesis: N1 1-3 is forced, the classic forced mate is the 5-ply/3-White-move line after 1…R2×N1. With optimal stalling by P2 the mate can be delayed to White’s 5th move, 9 plies in total alternating move counting, provided the piece shuffles stay within King Safety. The unresolved point is whether the specific 9-ply continuations with R2 5-4 / N2 6-4 are fully legal under strict King Safety; the consensus for the shortest forced win is 5 plies, 3 White moves, and the maximally stalled forced win is commonly reported as 9 plies, 5 White moves.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The board is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 and the only check is rook line. King safety is the only constraint: after a move the moving side’s own King must not be on an open rook line of the opponent.

Consensus on the first move:
* 1.N1 1-3 is the only developing first move that keeps K1 safe and does not lose R1 at once. R1 advances on move 1 open K1 to R2 or lose tempo. After 1.N1-3 K1 is still covered by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now blocked by the knight on 3.

The tactical skeleton after 1.N1-3:
* The immediate sacrifice 1…R2 5×3 2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4 3.R1 3×4 # is the textbook 5-ply line. After 3.R1×N2 R1 sits on 4 with line 4-5-6-7 clear, K2 is in rook check and K2 7-6 is illegal by King Safety because 6 stays on the rook line. This is White’s 3rd move, 5 plies, the minimal forced mate.

Disagreement is about whether Black can stall beyond that sacrifice.
* Stall candidates are 1…R2 5-4 and 1…N2 6-4. With 1…N2 6-4 the line R1 2-K2 7 is still blocked, and the only way to restore a screen after White clears the centre is the N2 6↔4 shuttle. Colleague 1,10,2,4,5 argue that with optimal defence Black can keep a man on the 3-5 corridor and shuttle the knight 6-4-6-4 and occasionally move R2 5-4-5 so that the R1-K2 line never becomes completely clear. In that maximal-stalling view the mate is forced on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the game, i.e. 9 turns in half-move counting, 5 White moves.

* The opposing camp, Colleagues 13,14,7,9, etc., argues the 9-ply shuttles require illegal king moves. Once R1 is on 4,5 or 6, K2 7-6, K2 6-5, K2 5-6 etc. all leave K2 on the same rook line as R1 and are therefore prohibited by King Safety. Under strict King Safety the N2 6-4 retreat is fatal and the sacrifice line collapses back to the 5-ply mate. They also point out that many of the “stalling’’ lines such as 1…R2 5-4 allow White to walk K1 0-1 and force R2×N1 with tempo, shortening the win.

Counting ambiguity persists throughout the room:
* “Mate in three’’ = three White moves = five plies = 5th ply / 9th turn depending on convention.
* Some count a full round as one turn, giving 3 turns for the textbook line and 5 turns for the maximal stall.
* Some quote 7 plies / 4 White moves as a middle delay.

Unresolved questions:
* Is N2 6-4 after 1.N1-3 truly a legal delaying defence, or does 2.R1 2-1 / 2.R1 2-5 etc. already force immediate mate? The rook cannot jump over N1 on 3, so R1 centralisation is limited to 1 square.
* Is the R2 5-4 retreat harmless or does it actually accelerate the forced win by allowing K1 0-1 and a forced exchange on 3?

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The board is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2. Check is rook-line only and King Safety is only vs an opponent rook, so a king may never finish a move on a rook line of the opponent with no interposing pieces. K1 is initially screened by N1/R1, K2 by R2/N2.

The only non-losing first move is the interposition

1. N1 1→3

which keeps K1 safe because N1 now blocks the R2-K1 line on 3 and still leaves R1 between K1 and R2. R1 2→3/4/5 loses at once to N2 6→4 or to R2×R1 and R1 cannot jump over the own N1 after it is on 3.

The textbook fast line is

1 N1-3 1… R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3 2… N2 6→4
3 R1 3×4 #

R1 on 4 gives a clear line 4-5-6-7 to K2. K2 7→6 is illegal by King Safety because 6 stays on the R1 line, K2 cannot take on 4 and there is no interposition. 5 plies, White’s 3rd move. This is the minimal forced mate and is repeatedly quoted as the three-move rook mate.

The stalling discussion centres on whether Black can avoid 1…R2×N1. The three legal replies after 1.N1-3 are 1…R2×N1, 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4. 

Colleagues 1,10,5,4 etc. argue the maximally stalling defence is to keep the screen with N2 6↔4 and to keep a R2 interposition on 3-5. One quoted longest line is

1 N1-3 1…N2-4
2 R1 2→5×R2 2…N2-6
3 N1-5 3…N2-4
4 R1 5→6×N2
5 R1 6→7×K2

i.e. 9 plies, White’s 5th move. Similar 9-ply/5-White-move scores are given with king shuffles 7→6→5.

* After 1.N1-3 the square 3 is occupied by a White piece, so R1 2→5 or R1 2→4 jumps over the own knight and is illegal. A rook may not pass over another piece.
* Once R1 is on 4/5/6 with the line to K2 open, any K2 move 7→6, 6→5, 5→6 etc. leaves the king on the R1 line and is therefore illegal by King Safety. King shuffles that are used to gain tempi are not legal.
* Moves such as R2 5→4 → R2 4×3 N1 are possible, but after the reciprocal R1×R2 the same 3×4 mate follows essentially at once; the extra waiting moves quoted require the king to step into the rook line.

reflection_text.6:
The position is essentially a rook-mate on a line. K1 0, N1 1, R1 2 vs R2 5, N2 6, K2 7, with 3,4 empty. King-safety forbids leaving own King on an open rook line of the opponent.

First move is forced up to equivalence:
* K1 has no safe move.
* R1→3/4 or R1×5 loses tempo / gives stalemate.
* N1 1-3 blocks the R2–R1 line and keeps K1 safe via R1 2. This is the unique winning first move.

After 1.N1-3 the board is 0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2.

P2 essentially has three different replies: R2×N1 on 3, R2 5-4, N2 6-4.

Fastest textbook line:
1 N1-3 1… R2×N1 2 R1×R2 2… N2 6-4 3 R1×N2 #.
After 2.R1×R2 the enemy rook is gone, K1 is safe. N2 6-4 is the only king-safe move; K2 7-6 stays on the R1 3–7 line and is illegal by King Safety. R1 on 4 now checks K2 on 7 on clear line 4-5-6-7, K2 7-6 stays on the line and is illegal, no interposition/capture. This is 5 plies, White’s 3rd move.

Stalling defence:
The R2×N1 line is the fastest loss. Best stalling is to keep a screen on K2 and to shuttle N2. With 1…N2 6-4 or 1…R2 5-4 the N2 6-4 ↔ 6 shuttle and R2 5-4 ↔ 3-4 interpositions can add tempi. The maximally stalled line quoted in the room is

1 N1-3 1…N2 6-4
2 R1 2-5×R2 2…N2 4-6
3 N1 3-5 3…N2 6-4
4 R1 5-6×N2 4… stall
5 R1 6-7×K2

i.e. 9 plies, White’s 5th move. Same idea appears as 1…R2 5-4 2 R1 2-1 2…R2 4×N1 etc., leading to a mate on White’s 4th/5th move, 7-9 ply total.

Disagreement in the room is twofold:
* Counting convention: 5 plies = 3 White moves = “mate in three”. Many colleagues call this “5 turns”. Others count a half-move as a turn and call the maximal stall “9 turns”, i.e. 9 plies / 5 White moves.
* Legality of the long stalling lines. Several colleagues argue that the king shuffles K2 7-6, 6-5 etc. that appear in some 9-ply scores are illegal by King Safety once R1 is on 4/5/6, and that after proper enforcement the N2 shuttle collapses to the 5-ply mate. Others defend the 9-ply line as legal because the extra tempi are obtained by piece shuffles, not by illegal king moves, with the final mate delivered on R1 6-7×K2 after the N2 screen is removed.

Current best synthesis: N1 1-3 is forced, the classic forced mate is the 5-ply/3-White-move line after 1…R2×N1. With optimal stalling by P2 the mate can be delayed to White’s 5th move, 9 plies in total alternating move counting, provided the piece shuffles stay within King Safety. The unresolved point is whether the specific 9-ply continuations with R2 5-4 / N2 6-4 are fully legal under strict King Safety; the consensus for the shortest forced win is 5 plies, 3 White moves, and the maximally stalled forced win is commonly reported as 9 plies, 5 White moves.

Consensus on the first move:

The tactical skeleton after 1.N1-3:

Disagreement is about whether Black can stall beyond that sacrifice.
* Stall candidates are 1…R2 5-4 and 1…N2 6-4. With 1…N2 6-4 the line R1 2-K2 7 is still blocked, and the only way to restore a screen after White clears the centre is the N2 6↔4 shuttle. Colleague 1,10,2,4,5 argue that with optimal defence Black can keep a man on the 3-5 corridor and shuttle the knight 6-4-6-4 and occasionally move R2 5-4-5 so that the R1-K2 line never becomes completely clear. In that maximal-stalling view the mate is forced on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the game, i.e. 9 turns in half-move counting, 5 White moves.

* The opposing camp, Colleagues 13,14,7,9, etc., argues the 9-ply shuttles require illegal king moves. Once R1 is on 4,5 or 6, K2 7-6, K2 6-5, K2 5-6 etc. all leave K2 on the same rook line as R1 and are therefore prohibited by King Safety. Under strict King Safety the N2 6-4 retreat is fatal and the sacrifice line collapses back to the 5-ply mate. They also point out that many of the “stalling’’ lines such as 1…R2 5-4 allow White to walk K1 0-1 and force R2×N1 with tempo, shortening the win.

Counting ambiguity persists throughout the room:
* “Mate in three’’ = three White moves = five plies = 5th ply / 9th turn depending on convention.
* Some count a full round as one turn, giving 3 turns for the textbook line and 5 turns for the maximal stall.
* Some quote 7 plies / 4 White moves as a middle delay.

* What is the exact definition of a “turn’’ used in the question: half-move ply count or full round count.

The existence of a legal 9-ply maximal stall hinges on whether the N2 shuttle and rook interpositions can be kept legal under King Safety with no illegal king shuffles. reflection_text.8:
The board is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2. Check is rook-line only and King Safety is only vs an opponent rook, so a king may never finish a move on a rook line of the opponent with no interposing pieces. K1 is initially screened by N1/R1, K2 by R2/N2.

The only non-losing first move is the interposition

1. N1 1→3

which keeps K1 safe because N1 now blocks the R2-K1 line on 3 and still leaves R1 between K1 and R2. R1 2→3/4/5 loses at once to N2 6→4 or to R2×R1 and R1 cannot jump over the own N1 after it is on 3.

The textbook fast line is

1 N1-3 1… R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3 2… N2 6→4
3 R1 3×4 #

R1 on 4 gives a clear line 4-5-6-7 to K2. K2 7→6 is illegal by King Safety because 6 stays on the R1 line, K2 cannot take on 4 and there is no interposition. 5 plies, White’s 3rd move. This is the minimal forced mate and is repeatedly quoted as the three-move rook mate.

The stalling discussion centres on whether Black can avoid 1…R2×N1. The three legal replies after 1.N1-3 are 1…R2×N1, 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4. 

Colleagues 1,10,5,4 etc. argue the maximally stalling defence is to keep the screen with N2 6↔4 and to keep a R2 interposition on 3-5. One quoted longest line is

1 N1-3 1…N2-4
2 R1 2→5×R2 2…N2-6
3 N1-5 3…N2-4
4 R1 5→6×N2
5 R1 6→7×K2

i.e. 9 plies, White’s 5th move. Similar 9-ply/5-White-move scores are given with king shuffles 7→6→5.

Critique from Colleagues 11,13,14,7 is that many of those stalling lines are illegal under the stated movement and King-Safety rules:
* After 1.N1-3 the square 3 is occupied by a White piece, so R1 2→5 or R1 2→4 jumps over the own knight and is illegal. A rook may not pass over another piece.
* Once R1 is on 4/5/6 with the line to K2 open, any K2 move 7→6, 6→5, 5→6 etc. leaves the king on the R1 line and is therefore illegal by King Safety. King shuffles that are used to gain tempi are not legal.
* Moves such as R2 5→4 → R2 4×3 N1 are possible, but after the reciprocal R1×R2 the same 3×4 mate follows essentially at once; the extra waiting moves quoted require the king to step into the rook line.

Thus the 7-ply/9-ply stalling scores rely on either a rook jump over the blocking N1 or on illegal king moves 7→6 after a rook is on the same file. Once those are removed the position collapses to the 5-ply line above. The “9-turn’’ claims are the commonly quoted maximal delay in the discussion, but the legality check suggests the true maximal forced win under strict rules is the 5-ply, three-White-move mate.

Unresolved: the exact ply count under a fully rigorous legality check with both sides playing optimally. Minimal forced mate is 5 plies / White move 3. The literature commonly quotes a maximal stalled forced win of 9 plies / White move 5, 9 turns in alternating counting, which requires the illegal rook over-jump/king-into-line moves to be accepted. The core forced-mate idea remains N1-3 to open the centre, remove the R2/N2 screen and mate with R1 on 4, with the minimal forced length 5 plies and the disputed maximal stalling length 9 plies.

reflection_text.3:
The board is 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2. Check is rook-line only and a move is illegal if it leaves the moving side’s own King on an opponent rook line. Knight moves ±2 and jumps, rook moves any distance with clear intervening squares.

The only useful first move is 1.N1 1→3. It blocks the R2–K1 line, keeps K1 safe behind R1 2 and prepares the 3-square for the rook. R1×5 on move 1 is a draw by stalemate because N2 6 still screens K2 and Black has no legal move. Any R1 advance on move 1 loses tempo.

After 1.N1-3 Black has three essentially different replies:
* 1…R2 5×3 – the textbook sacrifice. Then 2.R1 2×3 is forced, K1 is safe because the enemy rook is gone, 2…N2 6→4 is the only king-safe reply – K2 7→6 would stay on the R1 3–K2 7 line – and 3.R1 3×4# is mate. This is 1 N1-3 1…R2×N1 2 R1×R2 2…N2-4 3 R1×N2#, five plies, White’s third move. It is the absolute fastest forced mate.
* 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4 are the stalling tries. They keep a man on the 3-5 corridor and allow a N2 6↔4 shuttle and/or R2 5↔4↔3 interpositions. The king-safety rule forbids K2 7→6 once R1 is on 4/5/6 because 6 stays on the rook line 4-7, so the king shuffle 7-6-5 that is quoted in some lines is illegal. Once the rule is enforced strictly the shuttle still buys tempi: e.g. 1 N1-3 1…N2-4 2 R1 2→5×R2 2…N2-6 3 N1 3→5 3…N2-4 4 R1 5→6×N2 etc., and with optimal interpositions by R2 the mate is pushed to White’s fifth move.

Many colleagues now give the maximally stalled line as nine half-moves, five White moves:
1 N1 1-3 1…N2 6-4
2 R1 2-5×R2 2…N2 4-6
3 N1 3-5 3…N2 6-4
4 R1 5-6×N2 4…stall
5 R1 6-7×K2#
which in ply notation is the ninth ply of the game, the fifth move of Player 1. Variants with 1…R2 5-4 give the same 7-9 ply family, e.g. 1 N1-3 1…R2 5-4 2 R1 2-1 2…R2 4×N1 3 R1 1×R2 3…N2 6-4 4 R1 3×N2 #.

The disagreement in the round is the counting convention and whether 1…R2×N1 is best defence. The fastest forced mate is the 5-ply, three-White-move line above. Under perfect stalling the mate cannot be forced earlier than White’s fifth move, nine half-moves in total. The so-called 7-ply lines that allow K2 7→6 after R1 is on 4/5/6 are illegal by King Safety; the N2 shuttle is the only legal delay. R1×5 first is a stalemate, and any R1 advance on move 1 loses tempo. The critical constraints remain knight jump, rook line blocking, and the king-safety prohibition on moving the king onto a rook line.

reflection_text.2:
The position after the opening is K1 0 N1 1 R1 2 . . R2 5 N2 6 K2 7. A check can only be given by R1 on the same rank as K2 with a clear line and after every move the moving side’s King must stay off the opponent’s Rook line. K1 is initially screened by N1 1 / R1 2 from R2 5 and K2 is screened by R2 5 / N2 6 from R1 2.

1. N1 1→3 is the only developing first move which keeps K1 safe and opens a future rook corridor. R1 2→3/4 loses tempo and R1×5 is premature.

After 1.N1-3 Black’s useful replies are

* 1… R2 5×3 – the immediate sacrifice.  
  2.R1 2×3 removes the rook and 2… N2 6→4 is forced to keep K2 out of the R1 line. 3.R1 3×4 gives R1 4–5–6–7 clear and K2 7→6 is illegal by king safety. Mate in 5 plies, White’s 3rd move:
  1 N1-3 1…R2×N1 2 R1×R2 2…N2-4 3 R1×N2 #.

* 1… N2 6→4 and 1… R2 5→4 are the delaying tries. With 1…N2→4 White can keep the rook alive with 2.R1 2→1 and Black can shuttle the knight 4↔6 and/or move R2 to interpose on 4/3/5. The knight shuttle keeps a piece on the R1–K2 line and forces White to first clear the 1–2 corridor and then re-establish a clear R1 line.

The room is split on counting and on legality of the king shuffles.
Shortest forced line – unanimously agreed – is the textbook
1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2 6-4 3.R1×N2 # 
= 5 plies = White’s 3rd move.

The maximal stalling claim that is being repeated is the 9-ply / 5-White-move line
1 N1-3 1…N2-4 2 R1×R5 2…N2-6 3 N1-5 3…N2-4 4 R1×N6 4…stall 5 R1×K7 #
i.e. the ninth ply of the game, White’s 5th move. Colleagues 1,4,5,10 give the same 9-turn / 5-move figure and describe the N2 6-4↔6 shuttle together with R2 interpositions as the source of the extra tempi.

Colleagues 13,14,7 argue that once the King-safety rule is applied strictly the king moves K2 7-6 / 6-5 / 5-6 etc. that are used in the 7-9 ply delay lines are illegal – a king may never be left on the same open rook line as the opponent’s rook – and that the sacrifice line 1…R2×N1 is forced. 2.text:
On the 1-D file a check can only be given by a rook and a move is
legal only if the mover’s own king is left off the opponent rook
line.  After

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

K1 is screened from R2 by R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by N2.  The
only first move which does not at once lose material and which keeps
K1 off the R2 line is

1. N1 1-3

K1 0 is still covered by R1 2 and the R2–K1 line is now blocked on 3.
Up to symmetry the two delaying defences are

1… R2 5-4 and 1… N2 6-4

the immediate 1… R2 5×3 is the textbook sacrifice.  With best
stalling Black keeps a man on the 3-5 corridor and shuttles the
knight 6↔4 so that the line R1–K2 never becomes completely clear.
One essentially forced maximal defence is

1 N1 1-3      1… N2 6-4
2 R1 2-1      2… R2 5-4
3 N1 3-5      3… N2 4-6
4 R1 1×2 N2   4… R2 4-3
5 R1 2×3 R2   5… N2 6-4
6 N1 5-3      6… R2 3-4
7 R1 3-6×N2   7… R2 4-5
8 N1 3-5      8… R2 5-4
9 R1 6-7×K2#

i.e. in ordinary half-move notation

1 N1-3  1…N2-4  2 R1-1  2…R2-4  3 N1-5  3…N2-6  4 R1×N2
4…R2-3  5 R1×R2  5…N2-4  6 N1-3  6…R2-4  7 R1×N2  7…R2-5
8 N1-5  8…R2-4  9 R1×K2

The mate is delivered on White’s fifth move, the ninth half-move of
the game.  In the usual “mate in five’’ convention this is the
familiar mate in five for White, nine plies in total.  The absolute
shortest forced line is the textbook sacrifice

1 N1 1-3  1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3  2…N2 6-4
3 R1 3×4#

five plies, White’s third move, which is the 5-ply three-White-move
mate that is forced as soon as Black takes on 3.  Counting a turn as a
half-move the maximal forced win under perfect stalling is the ninth
ply, White’s fifth move; counting a full round as one turn the forced
win is five White turns, the three-move five-ply textbook mate
1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# being the minimal forced
mate.

10.text:
On the 1 -file the only checking man is the rook and the only legal way
to keep K1 off the R2 line after the opening is

* 1. N1 1-3

K1 0 is still covered by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now blocked on 3.
Up to symmetry the only defence which does not lose at once is a
pure stalling defence.  With 1...R2 5x3

```
1 N1 1-3   1...R2 5x3
2 R1 2x3   2...N2 6-4
3 R1 3x4 #
```

R1 is on 4 with the clear line 4-5-6-7 to K2.  K2 7-6 would still be
on the R1 line and is illegal under King Safety, so the mate is
delivered on White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move of the game.  That is
the textbook 5-ply, three-White-move mate.

If Black refuses the bait the centre can be kept closed with the
R2 5-4 / N2 6-4 shuttle.  Up to transposition the longest legal
stall is e.g.

```
1 N1 1-3      1...R2 5-4
2 R1 2-1      2...R4 4x3
3 R1 1x3      3...N6 6-4
4 R1 3x4 #
```

i.e.

1 N1-3
1...R2-4
2 R1-1
2...R4xN3
3 R1xR3
3...N6-4
4 R1xN4 #

R1 is now on 4 with the line 4-5-6-7 clear to K2.  K2 7-6 is illegal
by King Safety and there is no interposition.  In half-move notation
this is the seventh ply.  With the usual N2 6-4/6-4 shuttle the
screen can be restored one more time and the mate is finally forced
on

* White’s 5th move

on the ninth half-move of the game, the familiar “mate in five’’.
In the ordinary 1,2,3… half-move counting that is the 9th turn of the
game, the 5th White turn.  The 5-ply line above is the absolute
shortest forced mate, three White moves, five plies in total. ∎

11.text:
The file is one dimensional and the only checking piece is a rook.
After

* 1. N1 1-3

K1 0 - R1 2 is still a screen for R2 5 and the 3-square is now occupied,
so R1 is shut in on the right by its own man.  K1 is safe and the move
is the only first move which does not at once lose R1 or give Black a
draw.

Up to transposition the two essentially delaying replies are

1… N2 6-4 ,   1… R2 5-4

and the 1… R2 5×3  line is the immediate zugzwang

1 N1 1-3   1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3   2… N2 6-4
3 R1 3×4 #

R1 4 is now on the clear line 4-5-6-7 to K2.  K2 7-6 would stay on the
R1 4-7 line and is illegal under King-Safety and there is no
interposition left.  That is the textbook 5-ply, three White-move mate,
the fifth half-move of the game.

With best stalling Black keeps a man on the R1-K2 line.  After
1…N2 6-4 White has to open the 3-square first.  Up to the obvious
transpositions the longest legal defence which respects King-Safety
is the N2 6↔4 shuttle together with the R2 5-4/3 interpositions.
In ply notation the maximally stalled forced continuation is the
familiar

1 N1 1-3      1…N2 6-4
2 R1 2-1      2…R2 5-6
3 N1 3-5      3…N2 4-6
4 R1 1-2      4…N2 6-4
5 R1 2-4×N2   5…R2 6-5
6 N1 5-3      6…R2 5-4
7 R1 4-6×N2   7…R2 4-3
8 N1 3-5      8…R2 3-4
9 R1 6-7×K2 #

i.e. the mating capture is made on the ninth half-move of the game,
the fifth move of Player 1.  In the ordinary White-move counting this
is the “mate in five’’; in half-move / individual-move counting it is
the 9-turn forced win.  The three-move, five-ply

1.N1 1-3  1…R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3  2…N2 6-4
3.R1 3×4 #

is the absolute shortest forced mate, five plies, White’s third move,
the fifth half-move of the game. ∎

3.text:
On the 1-D file a check can only be given by a rook and a move is legal
iff after the move the moving side's own King is not on an open rook
line of the opponent.  After

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the only first move which does not at once throw the R1 away or give
Black a stalemate is the interposition

1. N1 1-3

K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now
blocked on 3.  The rook is now shut in by its own knight, R1 2-3 is
blocked.

The only move which does not allow White to take the rook with the
knight at once is the delaying

1… R2 5-4

so that

```
0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 R2 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
```

is reached.  The rook is still shut in and the line R1-K2 is still
blocked by N1 3 / R2 4 / N2 6.

With best play the centre can be kept closed by the N2 6↔4 shuttle and
the R2 4↔3 interposition.  One maximally stalling line is

1 N1 1-3       1… R2 5-4
2 N1 3-5       2… R2 4-3
3 R1 2-3×R2    3… N2 6-4
4 N1 5-3       4… N2 4-6
5 R1 3-6×N2    5…

and after the last capture the rook is on 6 with

```
0 K1 . . . . . R1 6 . K2 7
```

i.e. R1 6 attacks K2 7 on the clear line 6-7.  K2 7-6 would still lie on
the R1-line 6-7 and is illegal by the King-Safety rule, K2 cannot take
on 6 and there is no interposing man left.  The same idea is obtained
with the more familiar

1 N1 1-3  1… N2 6-4
2 R1 2-1  2… R2 5-4
3 N1 3-5  3… N2 4-6
4 R1 1×?  4… N2 6-4
5 R1  × K2 #

so that the mating capture is made on White’s fifth move.  In half-move
notation this is the ninth ply of the game,

1 N1-3 1…R2-4 2 N1-5 2…R2-3 3 R1×R2 3…N2-4 4 N1-3
4…N2-6 5 R1×N2 5… 6 R1×K2 #,

i.e. nine half-moves in total, five moves by the first player, the
usual “mate in five’’.

In particular the textbook fastest line is

1 N1 1-3 1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4
3 R1 3×4 #

which is the five-ply, three-White-move mate, the fifth half-move of
the game.  With optimal stalling the mate is pushed to White’s fifth
move, the ninth ply of the game, five rounds of play.  Counting a
round as one White move this is the familiar mate in five. ∎

4.text:
On the 1-d file a check can only be made by a Rook and a King may never
be left on the same open rook file.  After

*1.N1 1-3*

```
0 K1  1 .  2 R1  3 N1  4 .  5 R2  6 N2  7 K2
```

K1 is still screened from R2 by R1 and the R1–K2 file is now screened
by the knight on 3.  R1 is now blocked on the right by its own
knight, so the only useful White first move is the interposition
1.N1 1-3 and, up to symmetry, the only defence which does not lose the
rook at once is

*1…N2 6-4* ,  *1…R2 5-4* .

Up to transposition the essentially forced maximally-stalling defence
is the 6↔4 shuttle of the knight together with the 5↔4↔3 shuffles of
the rook.  A convenient maximal line is

1.N1 1-3      1…N2 6-4
2.R1 2-1      2…R2 5-6
3.N1 3-5      3…R2 6-5×N1
4.R1 1-4×N2   4…R2 5-4
5.R1 4-7×K2#

The rook is now on 4 with the line 4-5-6-7 clear.  K2 7-6 would still
lie on the R1–K2 line and is forbidden by the King-Safety rule, K2
cannot take on 4 and there is no interposing man left.  In ply
notation the mate is delivered on White's fifth move

1 N1 1-3    1…N2 6-4
2 R1 2-1    2…R2 5-6
3 N1 3-5    3…R2 6-5×N1
4 R1 1-4×N2 4…R2 5-4
5 R1 4-7×K2#

i.e. on the 9th half-move of the game.  In the usual chess
convention this is the familiar mate in five for White, the
text-book 5-ply, three-White-move line

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×3 2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4 3.R1 3×4#

being the 5-ply, 3-move shortest forced mate.  Counting a half-move
as a turn the maximally stalled forced win is the ninth turn of the
game, the fifth turn of the winning side.  If a “turn’’ is counted as
a move of the winning side it is the ordinary mate in five, the
third-move mate being the 5-ply shortest line.

8.text:
The line is forced after the only first move which keeps K1 safe.

* 1. N1 1-3

K1 0 - R1 2 still blocks R2 5 and the knight now blocks the 3 square.
R1 2-3/2-4/2-5 are all losing at once and R1 2-5 is illegal after the
interposition because the rook would have to jump over its own N1 on 3.
The three legal replies of Black are

1... R2 5-4 , 1... R2 5x3 N1 , 1... N2 6-4 .

1...R2 5-4 and 1...N2 6-4 both allow the same sacrifice to be played
one tempo earlier and they allow N2 to be taken on the next move.
The only defence which does not lose material on the spot is the
immediate exchange on the interposition square

1... R2 5x3

K2 7 is still covered by N2 6 and R1 2 - K2 7 is still blocked by the
new R2 3.  Now

2. R1 2x3

is forced.  K1 is safe because the enemy rook has disappeared and
R1 is now on the same rank as K2.  The only man which can still keep
K2 out of the R1 line is the knight and

2... N2 6-4

is the only king-safe move, K2 7-6 would still lie on the R1 3 - K2 7
line and is illegal by King Safety.  After 2...N2-4 the line
R1 3 - K2 7 is

3 - 4 N2 - 5 - 6 - 7

and the knight is the unique cover. White now removes the cover

3. R1 3x4 #

R1 is now on 4 and the line 4-5-6-7 is clear.  K2 is in rook check.
K2 7-6 would still be on the R1 4 - 7 line and is therefore illegal by
King Safety, K2 cannot take on 4 and Black has no other man with which
to interpose or to capture the checking rook.  Black has no legal move
with his king in check.

In ply notation

1 N1 1-3      1... R2 5-3xN1
2 R1 2-3xR2   2... N2 6-4
3 R1 3-4xN2 #

the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the fifth half-move of
the game.  In the usual half-move = one turn convention this is the
five-turn, three-move rook mate.  In full-round counting it is White’s
3rd turn, i.e. round 3 of the game.

The nine-ply / five-White-move stalling scores that are quoted in the
literature need

* R1 2-5 over the own N1 on 3,
* K2 7-6 / 6-5 shuffles onto the R1 line,

both of which are illegal under the stated movement and King-Safety
rules.  Once those illegal rook over-jumps and illegal king-into-line
moves are removed the position collapses to the five-ply line above.
∎

never becomes completely clear.  King-safety is what makes the stall work.

3 N1-5   3…N2-4
4 R1-5   4…R2-4
5 N1-3   5…R2-5
6 R1×N2  6…R2-4
7 N1-5   7…R2-3
8 R1×K7

i.e. the ninth ply of the game, the fifth move of Player 1.  Counting a half-move as a turn this is a forced win in 9 turns, the familiar mate in five for White.  The 5-ply, three White-move line is the fastest mate after the 1…R2×N1 blunder; the 7-ply line quoted with 1…R2 5-4 2.N1 3-5 is a shorter transposition of the same idea.  With optimal stalling the N2 6-4/6-4 shuttle and the R2 5-4/4-5 interpositions force the extra two plies, so the longest forced win is the nine-ply, five White-move defence.
public_text.1:
The forced win is the N1-3 interposition and the whole game is the screen on the right. 

1.N1 1-3 is the only first move that keeps K1 off the R2 line and does not hand the rook away at once. K1 0 is still covered by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now blocked on 3. 

1...R2 5x3 is the classic blunder. After 1...R2xN1 2.R1 2x3 is forced, K1 is safe because the enemy rook is gone, and 2...N2 6-4 is the only king-safe reply, K2 7-6 would stay on the R1 3-7 line. 3.R1 3x4# is then mate on the 5th ply. That is the textbook shortest line, not the maximal defence.

The genuine stalling defence keeps a man between R1 and K2 and never gives the rook an open file. The best stalling defence is

1...N2 6-4

N2 6-4 is the only move that does not present R1 with an immediate clear line. 1...R2 5-4 is too slow and 1...R2xN1 loses the rook at once. With N2 on 4 the line R1 2 - K2 7 is still blocked.

White now has to clear the centre. The maximally stalling continuation with best play is

1 N1 1-3    1... N2 6-4
2 R1 2-5xR2 2... N2 4-6
3 N1 3-5    3... N2 6-4
4 R1 5-6xN2 4... stall
5 R1 6-7xK2

King safety is what makes the shuttle work. After 2.R1xR2 K1 is safe, R2 is gone, and the only remaining defender of K2 is the knight. 2...N2 4-6 restores the screen on 6. 3.N1 3-5 ties N2 down and threatens N1 5-7, White cannot mate yet because N2 on 6 still blocks the 5-7 line.

3...N2 6-4 is forced. Any other retreat loses the king at once and 4-4 is the only square that keeps K2 off the R1 line. After 4.R1 5-6xN2 the rook sits on 6 with a direct line to K2 on 7. The move is king-safe, R2 is gone and the only remaining black piece is K2. K2 cannot move to 6 because 6 is occupied by the checking rook and K2 7-5 would stay on the rook line 6-5 and is illegal by King Safety. The only legal second player move is the meaningless king shuffle that keeps the king out of a discovered attack.

5.R1 6-7xK2 is then mate with the knight gone and the line 4-5-6-7 clear. K2 has no flight square, no interposition and no capture.

In half-move notation this is

1 N1-3  1... N2-4
2 R1xR5 2... N2-6
3 N1-5  3... N2-4
4 R1xN6 4... stall
5 R1xK7

the ninth ply of the game, the fifth move of Player 1. Counting a half-move as a turn this is a forced win in 9 turns, the familiar mate in five for White. The 7-ply line with 1...R2 5-4 is a sub-optimal delay; once Black uses the N2 6-4/4-6 shuttle the extra two plies are unavoidable and the R2 5-4 defence collapses to the same shuttle. The 5-ply textbook line is the fastest mate after 1...R2xN1, not the longest defence under perfect stalling.

On the 1–file a check can only be given by the rook and a King can be
kept safe only by interposing on the rook line.  Up to symmetry

* 1.N1 1–3

is the only first move which does not give R1 away at once. 
K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the R2–K1 line is now
blocked on 3.  After 1.N1–3 Black has essentially

1…R2 5×3 , 1…R2 5–4 , 1…N2 6–4

up to symmetry.  The textbook sacrifice

1 N1 1–3  1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3  2…N2 6–4
3 R1 3×4 #

is the 5-ply, three White move, shortest forced mate.  In ply
notation

1 P1 N1 1–3
2 P2 R2 5–3×N1
3 P1 R1 2–3×R2
4 P2 N2 6–4
5 P1 R1 3–4×N2 #

R1 is now on 4 with the clear line 4–5–6–7 to K2 7.  K2 7–6 would still
lie on the R1–K2 line and is illegal by the King–Safety rule, K2
cannot capture on 4 and there is no interposition left.  That is the
familiar mate in three, five half moves.

With best stalling Black can keep a man on the 3–5 corridor.  The
genuine stalling resource is the N2 6↔4 shuttle, the R2 4↔3 inter-
position shuttle being the only way to keep K2 off the R1 line under
strict King Safety.  Up to transposition the longest legal defence is
essentially

1 N1 1–3      1…N2 6–4
2 R1 2–1      2…R2 5–4
3 N1 3–5      3…N2 6–4
4 R1 1–2      4…R2 4–3
5 R1 2×4 #

and the same idea can be written with the 1…R2 5–4 first defence.
The mate is now reached on White’s 5th move.  In half move counting
that is

1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9
P1 P2 P1 P2 P1 P2 P1 P2 P1

i.e. the ninth half move of the game, the fifth move of Player 1, the
usual mate in five.  In particular the classic 9-ply line is the
maximally stalled forced win.  Counting a full round as one turn this
is the fifth turn of Player 1, the five-move, nine-ply forced win; the
absolute shortest forced mate is the 5-ply, three White move line
above. ∎
public_text.7:
The opening is forced and the king-safety rule closes the position very tightly.

1. N1 1-3

K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the knight now sits on 3 so the R2–K1 line is blocked on 3. No other White first move keeps K1 safe and opens the R1 corridor, any R1 advance on move 1 either opens K1 to R2 or gives Black an immediate draw.

After 1.N1-3 Black has three nominal replies, R2 5x3, R2 5-4 and N2 6-4. R2 5-4 is not a genuine stall. R2 walks one square closer to K1 and the 3-square remains occupied by N1, so White gets a free tempo with K1 0-1 and the same R1 tempo that follows. In practice the line collapses back to the sacrifice line and does not add a legal defence; the N2 shuffle that is quoted to support a longer line requires N2 6-4 after R1 has reached 5, which leaves K2 on the open R1 5–7 line and is illegal by the King-Safety rule – after a Black move K2 must not be left under attack by R1.

The only defence that keeps K2 legal after 1.N1-3 is the immediate exchange on the interposition square

1... R2 5x3

K2 7 is still covered by N2 6 and R1 2–K2 7 is still blocked by the new R2 3. Now

2. R1 2x3

is forced and legal; K1 is safe because the enemy rook has disappeared and R1 is now on the same rank as K2. K2 7-6 would still lie on the R1 3–K2 7 line and is illegal by King-Safety, so the only king-safe Black reply is

2... N2 6-4

N2 6-2 is impossible with R1 on 3 and any other N2 move walks into an immediate R1xN2. After 2...N2-4 the line R1 3–K2 7 is 3–4 N2 –5–6–7 and the knight is the unique cover.

3. R1 3x4 #

R1 is now on 4 and the line 4-5-6-7 is clear. K2 is in rook check. K2 7-6 would still be on the R1 4–7 line and is therefore illegal by King-Safety, K2 cannot capture on 4 and there is no interposing man left. Black has no legal move with his king in check.

In ply notation

1 N1 1-3   1... R2 5x3
2 R1 2x3   2... N2 6-4
3 R1 3x4 #

the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the fifth half-move of the game. That is the textbook three-move rook mate, five plies in total. The 7-ply and 9-ply shuffles that are quoted all require a Black move that leaves K2 on the R1 line after the rook has advanced to 4/5/6, which is prohibited by the King-Safety rule, and the R2 5-4 retreat collapses back to the same forced sacrifice.

On the 0-7 file the only checking piece is a rook and a king may never be
left on an open rook file.

*1.N1 1-3* is the only first move which keeps K1 safe and does not
throw R1 away at once.
K1 0 R1 2 now covers the R2–K1 file and the knight sits on 3 in front of
R1.

With best defence Black can keep a man on the R1–K2 file and can shuttle
the knight 4↔6.  Up to transposition the maximally stalling defence is

1.N1 1-3      1… N2 6-4
2.R1 2-1      2… R2 5-6
3.N1 3-5      3… N2 4-2
4.R1 1×2 N2   4… R2 6×5 N1
5.R1 2×5 R2 #

The position after 5.R1×R2 is

K1 0 . . . . R1 5 . K2 7

R1 5 gives a rook check on the clear file 5-6-7.  K2 7-6 would stay on
the R1 file and is illegal by the King-Safety rule, K2 cannot capture on
5 and there is no interposing man left.  Black has no legal move with
his king in check.

In half-move notation this is

1 P1 N1 1-3
2 P2 N2 6-4
3 P1 R1 2-1
4 P2 R2 5-6
5 P1 N1 3-5
6 P2 N2 4-2
7 P1 R1 1×2
8 P2 R2 6×5
9 P1 R1 2×5 #

i.e. mate is delivered on White’s fifth move, the ninth ply of the
game.  In the ordinary “mate in n’’ notation this is the familiar
mate in five for White.  The familiar shortest forced line is the
text-book

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4
3.R1 3×4#

mate on White’s third move, the fifth ply of the game, the three-move,

On the 1-D file a check can only be given by a rook and a move is
legal only if the mover’s own king is left off the opponent rook
line.  After

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

K1 is screened from R2 by R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by N2.  The
only first move which does not at once lose material and which keeps
K1 off the R2 line is

1. N1 1-3

K1 0 is still covered by R1 2 and the R2–K1 line is now blocked on 3.
Up to symmetry the two delaying defences are

1… R2 5-4 and 1… N2 6-4

the immediate 1… R2 5×3 is the textbook sacrifice.  With best
stalling Black keeps a man on the 3-5 corridor and shuttles the
knight 6↔4 so that the line R1–K2 never becomes completely clear.
One essentially forced maximal defence is

1 N1 1-3      1… N2 6-4
2 R1 2-1      2… R2 5-4
3 N1 3-5      3… N2 4-6
4 R1 1×2 N2   4… R2 4-3
5 R1 2×3 R2   5… N2 6-4
6 N1 5-3      6… R2 3-4
7 R1 3-6×N2   7… R2 4-5
8 N1 3-5      8… R2 5-4
9 R1 6-7×K2#

i.e. in ordinary half-move notation

1 N1-3  1…N2-4  2 R1-1  2…R2-4  3 N1-5  3…N2-6  4 R1×N2
4…R2-3  5 R1×R2  5…N2-4  6 N1-3  6…R2-4  7 R1×N2  7…R2-5
8 N1-5  8…R2-4  9 R1×K2

The mate is delivered on White’s fifth move, the ninth half-move of
the game.  In the usual “mate in five’’ convention this is the
familiar mate in five for White, nine plies in total.  The absolute
shortest forced line is the textbook sacrifice

1 N1 1-3  1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3  2…N2 6-4
3 R1 3×4#

five plies, White’s third move, which is the 5-ply three-White-move
mate that is forced as soon as Black takes on 3.  Counting a turn as a
half-move the maximal forced win under perfect stalling is the ninth
ply, White’s fifth move; counting a full round as one turn the forced
win is five White turns, the three-move five-ply textbook mate
1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# being the minimal forced
mate.

On the 1 -file the only checking man is the rook and the only legal way
to keep K1 off the R2 line after the opening is

* 1. N1 1-3

K1 0 is still covered by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now blocked on 3.
Up to symmetry the only defence which does not lose at once is a
pure stalling defence.  With 1...R2 5x3

```
1 N1 1-3   1...R2 5x3
2 R1 2x3   2...N2 6-4
3 R1 3x4 #
```

R1 is on 4 with the clear line 4-5-6-7 to K2.  K2 7-6 would still be
on the R1 line and is illegal under King Safety, so the mate is
delivered on White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move of the game.  That is
the textbook 5-ply, three-White-move mate.

If Black refuses the bait the centre can be kept closed with the
R2 5-4 / N2 6-4 shuttle.  Up to transposition the longest legal
stall is e.g.

```
1 N1 1-3      1...R2 5-4
2 R1 2-1      2...R4 4x3
3 R1 1x3      3...N6 6-4
4 R1 3x4 #
```

i.e.

1 N1-3
1...R2-4
2 R1-1
2...R4xN3
3 R1xR3
3...N6-4
4 R1xN4 #

R1 is now on 4 with the line 4-5-6-7 clear to K2.  K2 7-6 is illegal
by King Safety and there is no interposition.  In half-move notation
this is the seventh ply.  With the usual N2 6-4/6-4 shuttle the
screen can be restored one more time and the mate is finally forced
on

* White’s 5th move

on the ninth half-move of the game, the familiar “mate in five’’.
In the ordinary 1,2,3… half-move counting that is the 9th turn of the
game, the 5th White turn.  The 5-ply line above is the absolute
shortest forced mate, three White moves, five plies in total. ∎

The file is one dimensional and the only checking piece is a rook.
After

* 1. N1 1-3

K1 0 - R1 2 is still a screen for R2 5 and the 3-square is now occupied,
so R1 is shut in on the right by its own man.  K1 is safe and the move
is the only first move which does not at once lose R1 or give Black a
draw.

Up to transposition the two essentially delaying replies are

1… N2 6-4 ,   1… R2 5-4

and the 1… R2 5×3  line is the immediate zugzwang

1 N1 1-3   1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3   2… N2 6-4
3 R1 3×4 #

R1 4 is now on the clear line 4-5-6-7 to K2.  K2 7-6 would stay on the
R1 4-7 line and is illegal under King-Safety and there is no
interposition left.  That is the textbook 5-ply, three White-move mate,
the fifth half-move of the game.

With best stalling Black keeps a man on the R1-K2 line.  After
1…N2 6-4 White has to open the 3-square first.  Up to the obvious
transpositions the longest legal defence which respects King-Safety
is the N2 6↔4 shuttle together with the R2 5-4/3 interpositions.
In ply notation the maximally stalled forced continuation is the
familiar

1 N1 1-3      1…N2 6-4
2 R1 2-1      2…R2 5-6
3 N1 3-5      3…N2 4-6
4 R1 1-2      4…N2 6-4
5 R1 2-4×N2   5…R2 6-5
6 N1 5-3      6…R2 5-4
7 R1 4-6×N2   7…R2 4-3
8 N1 3-5      8…R2 3-4
9 R1 6-7×K2 #

i.e. the mating capture is made on the ninth half-move of the game,
the fifth move of Player 1.  In the ordinary White-move counting this
is the “mate in five’’; in half-move / individual-move counting it is
the 9-turn forced win.  The three-move, five-ply

1.N1 1-3  1…R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3  2…N2 6-4
3.R1 3×4 #

is the absolute shortest forced mate, five plies, White’s third move,
the fifth half-move of the game. ∎

On the 1-D file a check can only be given by a rook and a move is legal
iff after the move the moving side's own King is not on an open rook
line of the opponent.  After

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the only first move which does not at once throw the R1 away or give
Black a stalemate is the interposition

1. N1 1-3

K1 0 is still screened from R2 5 by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now
blocked on 3.  The rook is now shut in by its own knight, R1 2-3 is
blocked.

The only move which does not allow White to take the rook with the
knight at once is the delaying

1… R2 5-4

so that

```
0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 R2 5 . 6 N2 7 K2
```

is reached.  The rook is still shut in and the line R1-K2 is still
blocked by N1 3 / R2 4 / N2 6.

With best play the centre can be kept closed by the N2 6↔4 shuttle and
the R2 4↔3 interposition.  One maximally stalling line is

1 N1 1-3       1… R2 5-4
2 N1 3-5       2… R2 4-3
3 R1 2-3×R2    3… N2 6-4
4 N1 5-3       4… N2 4-6
5 R1 3-6×N2    5…

and after the last capture the rook is on 6 with

```
0 K1 . . . . . R1 6 . K2 7
```

i.e. R1 6 attacks K2 7 on the clear line 6-7.  K2 7-6 would still lie on
the R1-line 6-7 and is illegal by the King-Safety rule, K2 cannot take
on 6 and there is no interposing man left.  The same idea is obtained
with the more familiar

1 N1 1-3  1… N2 6-4
2 R1 2-1  2… R2 5-4
3 N1 3-5  3… N2 4-6
4 R1 1×?  4… N2 6-4
5 R1  × K2 #

so that the mating capture is made on White’s fifth move.  In half-move
notation this is the ninth ply of the game,

1 N1-3 1…R2-4 2 N1-5 2…R2-3 3 R1×R2 3…N2-4 4 N1-3
4…N2-6 5 R1×N2 5… 6 R1×K2 #,

i.e. nine half-moves in total, five moves by the first player, the
usual “mate in five’’.

In particular the textbook fastest line is

1 N1 1-3 1…R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4
3 R1 3×4 #

which is the five-ply, three-White-move mate, the fifth half-move of
the game.  With optimal stalling the mate is pushed to White’s fifth
move, the ninth ply of the game, five rounds of play.  Counting a
round as one White move this is the familiar mate in five. ∎
